q: According to the induced-fit model of enzyme action,
c: the active site changes shape to fit the substrate as it binds
the active site is a rigid shape that exactly matches the substrate
the substrate changes the enzyme's primary structure
the enzyme is consumed in the reaction
h: Compare it with the older lock-and-key model, in which the active site never changes.
w: In induced fit, the flexible active site adjusts its shape around the substrate, which explains why some enzymes accept a group of similar substrates. A rigid site is the lock-and-key model; enzymes are never consumed.
x: A rigid active site that exactly matches the substrate is the older lock-and-key model. Induced fit pictures a more flexible active site.
The primary structure is the amino acid sequence, held by covalent peptide bonds. Substrate binding does not change the sequence.
Enzymes are catalysts: they come out of the reaction unchanged and can be used again and again.

q: Urease catalyzes the hydrolysis of urea and no other compound. This is an example of
h: How many different substrates does urease accept?
w: An enzyme that acts on only one substrate shows absolute specificity. Group specificity means one functional group in many compounds; linkage means one bond type.
x: Group specificity means the enzyme acts on one type of functional group in many different compounds. Urease accepts only one compound.
Linkage specificity means the enzyme acts on one kind of bond wherever it occurs. Think about how many substrates urease accepts.
Stereochemical specificity means telling apart mirror-image forms (such as D and L). Nothing here is about mirror images.

q: Hexokinase moves a phosphate group from ATP to glucose. To which enzyme class does hexokinase belong?
h: Focus on what the enzyme does: it moves a group from one molecule to another.
w: Enzymes that move a functional group (here, phosphate) between molecules are transferases; kinases are a type of transferase. Hydrolases use water to split bonds.
x: A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. Here nothing is split by water; a phosphate is moved from ATP onto glucose.
An oxidoreductase catalyzes oxidation and reduction, such as moving hydrogen to NAD<sup>+</sup>. Moving a phosphate group is not a redox change.
An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule. Here a group moves from one molecule (ATP) to a different molecule (glucose).

q: A patient has a very high fever of 42 °C. What generally happens to the activity of the patient's enzymes?
c: It decreases because the enzymes begin to denature.
It increases without limit as temperature rises.
It stays the same because enzymes are catalysts.
It decreases because substrate molecules move more slowly.
h: Most human enzymes work best near 37 °C. What happens to proteins well above that?
w: Above the optimum temperature (~37 °C), enzymes start to lose their shape (denature), so activity drops. Molecules move faster, not slower, when hot.
x: Rate rises with temperature only up to the optimum. Enzymes are proteins, so well above about 37 °C something happens to their shape.
Being a catalyst does not make an enzyme immune to heat. Enzymes are proteins, and their shape depends on temperature.
Higher temperature makes molecules move faster, not slower. The drop in activity comes from a change in the enzyme itself.

q: Pepsin works best at about pH 2 in the stomach. When pepsin enters the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, its activity
h: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. What happens far from it?
w: pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum of 2, so the charges on its side chains change, its active site loses its shape, and its activity decreases sharply. Trypsin, with an optimum near pH 8, takes over there.
x: Moving away from an enzyme's optimum pH lowers activity. pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum of about 2.
pH changes the charges on side chains, which affects the active site's shape. A change from pH 2 to 8 is a big one.
A higher pH is not better for every enzyme. Each enzyme has its own optimum pH, and pepsin's is very acidic.

q: With a fixed amount of enzyme, the reaction rate stops increasing at very high substrate concentration because
c: all of the active sites are occupied
the enzyme is denatured by the substrate
h: Think about a fixed number of active sites working as fast as they can.
w: Once every enzyme molecule is bound to substrate, the enzyme is saturated, so adding more substrate cannot raise the rate. Adding more enzyme could.
x: Substrate does not denature the enzyme; heat, extreme pH and heavy metals do. The leveling off happens with a healthy enzyme.
The substrate is what the enzyme acts on, not an inhibitor. Think about how many active sites are available to work.
Products are made, not used up, as the reaction runs. The limit comes from the fixed amount of enzyme.

q: Methanol poisoning can be treated with ethanol, which binds to the active site of alcohol dehydrogenase and slows the formation of toxic formaldehyde. Ethanol is acting as a(n)
h: Where does ethanol bind, and does it resemble the substrate?
w: Ethanol resembles methanol and competes for the same active site: competitive inhibition. A noncompetitive inhibitor would bind elsewhere and could not be outcompeted.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site. Ethanol binds in the active site itself.
An irreversible inhibitor forms a permanent covalent bond with the enzyme. Ethanol binds reversibly and is eventually metabolized.
A coenzyme helps the enzyme do its job. Here ethanol slows the enzyme's action on methanol.

q: A noncompetitive inhibitor decreases an enzyme's activity by
c: binding at a site other than the active site and changing its shape
binding in the active site in place of the substrate
forming a covalent bond with the substrate molecule
raising the activation energy of the uncatalyzed reaction
h: Can adding more substrate overcome this type of inhibition? That tells you where it binds.
w: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site, distorting the enzyme so the active site no longer works; extra substrate does not help. Binding in the active site is competitive inhibition.
x: Binding in the active site in place of the substrate describes competitive inhibition, which can be overcome by more substrate.
Inhibitors act on the enzyme, not by bonding to the substrate molecule.
Inhibitors do not change the uncatalyzed reaction at all. They work by interfering with the enzyme itself.

q: Organophosphate insecticides and nerve agents form a covalent bond with the active site of acetylcholinesterase. This is an example of
h: A covalent bond to the active site permanently inactivates the enzyme.
w: Covalent modification of the active site is irreversible inhibition; acetylcholine then builds up at nerve synapses. Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly.
x: Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly and can be pushed out by more substrate. A covalent bond to the active site is permanent.
Allosteric activation speeds an enzyme up. These poisons shut acetylcholinesterase down.
Feedback control is the end product of a pathway slowing an early enzyme reversibly. These poisons are outside chemicals that bond covalently.

q: The end product of a metabolic pathway binds to an allosteric site on the first enzyme of the pathway and slows it down. This is called
h: The product “talks back” to the start of the pathway when enough has been made.
w: When enough end product is present, it inhibits the first enzyme allosterically, turning off its own production: feedback control. It binds a regulatory site, not the active site, so it is not competitive inhibition.
x: A competitive inhibitor binds in the active site. Here the end product binds an allosteric (regulatory) site instead.
Zymogen activation turns an inactive precursor into an active enzyme by cutting it. This question describes slowing an enzyme down.
Induced fit describes how an active site changes shape as substrate binds. It is not a way of regulating a pathway.

q: The coenzyme NAD<sup>+</sup> is made from which vitamin?
h: The “N” in NAD<sup>+</sup> refers to nicotinamide.
w: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide comes from niacin. Riboflavin forms FAD and pantothenic acid forms coenzyme A.
x: Riboflavin (B<sub>2</sub>) is used to make FAD, a different coenzyme. Think about what the "N" in NAD<sup>+</sup> stands for.
Pantothenic acid (B<sub>5</sub>) is used to make coenzyme A, not NAD<sup>+</sup>.
Vitamin C is an antioxidant needed for collagen formation. It is not the source of NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: How does an enzyme increase the rate of a reaction in the body?
c: It lowers the activation energy of the reaction
It raises the temperature of the reaction mixture
It makes the overall reaction more exothermic
It shifts the equilibrium toward the products
h: A catalyst changes the pathway, not the energies of the starting materials or products.
w: An enzyme provides a pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed at body temperature. It does not change ΔH or the equilibrium position; it speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally.
x: Enzymes do not heat the reaction; body temperature stays about 37 °C. They change the pathway the reaction follows.
A catalyst does not change ΔH. The energies of the reactants and products stay the same.
A catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not change the equilibrium position.

q: Statins such as atorvastatin (Lipitor) block HMG-CoA reductase, the liver enzyme that controls the pathway making cholesterol from acetyl CoA. A statin resembles the enzyme’s normal substrate and binds reversibly in its active site. A statin is therefore a(n)
h: It looks like the substrate and binds where the substrate binds.
w: An inhibitor that resembles the substrate and competes for the active site is a competitive inhibitor. With less cholesterol made, the liver removes more LDL from the blood. A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme; an irreversible inhibitor forms a covalent bond.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site. The statin binds in the active site and resembles the substrate.
An irreversible inhibitor forms a covalent bond. The question says the statin binds reversibly.
An activator speeds an enzyme up. Statins slow cholesterol production.

q: Penicillin irreversibly inhibits transpeptidase, an enzyme bacteria use to build their cell walls. Why does penicillin harm bacteria but not human cells?
c: Human cells have no cell walls, so they do not use this enzyme
Human cells break down penicillin before it can reach them
Human transpeptidase has an active site that penicillin cannot fit
Human substrates outcompete penicillin for the active site
h: An inhibitor can only harm cells that actually depend on the enzyme it blocks.
w: Penicillin bonds covalently to transpeptidase, so bacteria cannot cross-link their cell walls and they burst. Animal cells have no cell walls, so the target is absent in humans. Penicillin is an irreversible inhibitor, so substrate cannot outcompete it.
x: Penicillin does reach human cells; it circulates in the blood. The real question is whether human cells use this enzyme.
Humans do not have a transpeptidase for building cell walls. Ask what structure bacteria have that human cells lack.
Penicillin is an irreversible inhibitor, so substrate cannot outcompete it. Think about whether human cells even use this enzyme.

q: Damaged cells leak their proteins into the blood, so blood tests can show which tissue is injured. Troponin (a muscle protein) and the enzyme CK-MB (a form of creatine kinase) are concentrated in heart muscle, lipase in the pancreas, ALT in the liver, and amylase in the pancreas and salivary glands. A few hours after chest pain, a patient’s blood troponin and CK-MB rise sharply. Which tissue is most likely damaged?
h: Match the markers that rose to the tissue where they are concentrated.
w: Troponin and CK-MB are concentrated in heart muscle, so their rise after chest pain points to a heart attack. Troponin is the main heart-attack test used today; CK-MB is an older enzyme marker. High lipase would point to the pancreas and high ALT to the liver.
x: Lipase and amylase point to the pancreas. The markers that rose here are concentrated in a different tissue.
ALT is the liver marker. The markers that rose here are not ALT.
Amylase points to the salivary glands. Match troponin and CK-MB to the tissue where they are concentrated.

q: In β-oxidation, and in the citric acid cycle step succinate → fumarate, a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– group is oxidized to –CH=CH–. Which coenzyme accepts the hydrogen atoms in this type of reaction?
c: FAD, which is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>
NAD<sup>+</sup>, which is reduced to NADH
coenzyme A, which forms a thioester
NADPH, which is oxidized to NADP<sup>+</sup>
h: One oxidizing coenzyme turns C–OH into C=O; the other forms C=C double bonds. Which is which?
w: Forming a carbon–carbon double bond uses FAD → FADH2 (FAD is made from vitamin B2, riboflavin). NAD+ oxidizes C–OH groups to C=O, coenzyme A carries acyl groups, and NADPH is a reducing agent used in biosynthesis.
x: NAD<sup>+</sup> is used when a C–OH is oxidized to C=O. Forming a C=C double bond uses the other oxidizing coenzyme.
Coenzyme A carries acyl groups as thioesters; it does not accept hydrogen atoms in an oxidation.
NADPH is a reducing agent used in biosynthesis. This step is an oxidation, so the coenzyme must accept hydrogen, not give it.

q: An enzyme from the pancreas hydrolyzes the ester bonds of dietary triacylglycerols in the small intestine. What type of enzyme is it?
h: Enzyme names often come from the substrate plus “-ase.” What kind of biomolecule is a triacylglycerol?
w: A triacylglycerol is a lipid, so the enzyme is a lipase. Amylase digests starch, a protease digests proteins, and a nuclease digests nucleic acids.
x: Amylase hydrolyzes starch, a carbohydrate. A triacylglycerol is a different type of biomolecule.
A protease hydrolyzes the peptide bonds of proteins. Triacylglycerols contain ester bonds, not peptide bonds.
A nuclease hydrolyzes nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). Think about what class of biomolecule a triacylglycerol is.

q: In glycolysis, an enzyme converts glucose-6-phosphate into fructose-6-phosphate. Both have the formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>O<sub>9</sub>P<sup>2−</sup>. To which enzyme class does this enzyme belong?
h: The reactant and product have the same formula. What kind of change is that?
w: Only the arrangement of atoms changes (an aldose becomes a ketose), so the enzyme is an isomerase. No group moves to another molecule (transferase), and no water is added (hydrolase).
x: A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Here one molecule just rearranges, keeping the same formula.
A lyase adds or removes groups at a double bond, or breaks bonds without water. The formula here does not change at all.
A hydrolase adds water to split a molecule. The product has exactly the same formula as the reactant.

q: Aldolase splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (6 C) into two 3-carbon molecules by breaking a C–C bond, without adding water and without oxidation. To which enzyme class does aldolase belong?
h: Which class breaks (or forms) bonds without water and without a redox change?
w: A lyase cleaves C–C (or C–O, C–N) bonds without hydrolysis or oxidation, often forming double bonds or adding groups to them. A hydrolase would need water, and a ligase joins molecules using ATP.
x: A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. The question says no water is added.
An oxidoreductase catalyzes redox reactions. The question says there is no oxidation.
A ligase joins two molecules using energy from ATP. Aldolase splits one molecule into two.

q: Pyruvate carboxylase catalyzes the reaction below. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: Two molecules are joined into one, and ATP energy is spent to do it.
w: Joining two molecules (pyruvate + CO2) with energy from ATP hydrolysis is the job of a ligase. A lyase can add groups to double bonds but does not use ATP; a transferase only moves a group from one molecule to another.

f.text: pyruvate + CO<sub>2</sub> + ATP → oxaloacetate + ADP + P<sub>i</sub>

x: A lyase can add groups to a double bond, but it does not use ATP. This reaction spends ATP to join two molecules.
A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Here pyruvate and CO<sub>2</sub> are joined into one molecule with ATP energy.
An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule. Here two molecules are joined into one.

q: In a lab experiment, substrate is kept in large excess while the amount of enzyme is increased. How does a graph of reaction rate versus enzyme concentration look?
c: a straight line rising steadily as enzyme is added
a curve that rises and then levels off at a maximum
a bell-shaped curve with a peak at an optimum value
a line falling steadily as enzyme is added
h: With plenty of substrate, every new enzyme molecule finds substrate to work on. Is there anything to run out of?
w: When substrate is in excess, each added enzyme molecule works at full speed, so the rate is directly proportional to [E]: a straight, rising line. The leveling-off curve is the rate vs. [substrate] graph (active sites saturate); bell curves describe temperature and pH.
x: Leveling off is the rate vs. [substrate] graph, where active sites become saturated. Here substrate is always in excess.
Bell-shaped curves with an optimum describe temperature and pH. Changing the amount of enzyme does not have an optimum.
Adding more catalyst does not slow a reaction down. Each added enzyme molecule has plenty of substrate to work on.

q: An inhibitor slows an enzyme, but the inhibition disappears when a large excess of substrate is added. What type of inhibitor is it?
h: If substrate can “win,” the inhibitor and the substrate must be fighting over the same place.
w: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds the active site, so a high [substrate] outcompetes it. A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the active site's shape, so adding substrate does not help.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site, so adding more substrate does not help.
An irreversible inhibitor bonds permanently, so extra substrate cannot reverse it.
An activator speeds an enzyme up. This molecule slows the enzyme.

q: Which fat-soluble vitamin is correctly matched with its main function?
c: vitamin K: needed for blood clotting
vitamin D: needed for night vision
vitamin A: needed for blood clotting
vitamin K: needed for calcium absorption
h: Recall: A helps the eyes, D helps the bones, K is used for clotting (“K” for the German word Koagulation).
w: Vitamin K is needed to make clotting factors (newborns get a vitamin K shot for this reason). Vitamin A forms retinal for vision, and vitamin D (made in skin exposed to sunlight) increases calcium absorption for bones.
x: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for bones. Night vision depends on a different vitamin.
Vitamin A is used to make retinal for vision. Clotting depends on a different vitamin.
Calcium absorption is the job of vitamin D. Recall what the "K" (Koagulation) stands for.

q: Isocitrate dehydrogenase removes hydrogen from isocitrate and transfers it to NAD<sup>+</sup>. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: The name ends in “dehydrogenase.” What kind of reaction is removal of hydrogen?
w: Dehydrogenases catalyze oxidation–reduction reactions (substrate oxidized, NAD+ reduced), so they are oxidoreductases. Transferases move groups such as –NH2 or phosphate between molecules, which is a different reaction.
x: A transferase moves a group such as –NH<sub>2</sub> or phosphate between molecules. Removing hydrogen and giving it to NAD<sup>+</sup> is a different kind of reaction.
A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. No water is involved here.
An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule. Here hydrogen is removed and given to NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), measured in liver-function blood tests, moves an amino group from alanine to α-ketoglutarate. To which enzyme class does ALT belong?
h: An amino group is moved from one molecule to another, with no water, no redox and no ATP.
w: Moving a functional group (here –NH2) from one substrate to another is the job of a transferase. Oxidative deamination, which releases NH+4 using NAD+, would be an oxidoreductase reaction.
x: A lyase adds or removes groups at a double bond, or breaks bonds without water. Here a group is moved between two molecules.
A ligase joins two molecules using ATP energy. No ATP is used here.
An oxidoreductase moves electrons, usually with NAD<sup>+</sup> or FAD. No redox coenzyme is used in this reaction.

q: Which line lists a digestive enzyme with the nutrient it hydrolyzes and the organ where it mainly works?
h: Match each enzyme name to its substrate (amyl- = starch, lip- = fat), then check where that enzyme works.
w: Pepsin hydrolyzes proteins in the acidic stomach. Salivary amylase acts on starch, not fats; pancreatic lipase acts on fats, not starch; trypsin works in the small intestine, not the mouth.
x: Salivary amylase does work in the mouth, but it digests starch, not triacylglycerols (fats).
Pancreatic lipase does work in the small intestine, but it digests fats, not starch.
Trypsin does digest proteins, but it works in the small intestine, not the mouth.

q: Fumarase adds a water molecule across the C=C double bond of fumarate to form malate. To which enzyme class does fumarase belong?
h: Hydrolases use water to split a bond into two molecules. Which class adds groups (like H<sub>2</sub>O) to a double bond, or removes them to form one?
w: Adding H2O to a C=C without splitting the molecule is the job of a lyase. A hydrolase would use water to cut one molecule into two pieces, which does not happen here.
x: A hydrolase uses water to split one molecule into two. Here water is added across a double bond and the molecule stays in one piece.
An oxidoreductase catalyzes redox reactions with a coenzyme such as NAD<sup>+</sup>. Adding H<sub>2</sub>O across a C=C is not a redox step here.
An isomerase rearranges atoms without changing the formula. Malate has one more H<sub>2</sub>O than fumarate.

q: Glutamine synthetase joins glutamate and NH+4 to form glutamine, using the energy of ATP hydrolysis. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: Which class joins two molecules into one and needs energy from ATP to do it?
w: Joining two molecules with energy from ATP is the definition of a ligase (a synthetase). A transferase only moves a group from one molecule to another.
x: A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Here two molecules are joined into one, and ATP is spent to do it.
A lyase adds or removes groups at a double bond and does not use ATP. This reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis.
A hydrolase uses water to split a molecule apart. This reaction builds a bigger molecule instead.

q: Phosphoglucomutase converts glucose-1-phosphate into glucose-6-phosphate by moving the phosphate group to a different carbon of the same molecule. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: Compare the formulas of the substrate and the product. Is a group moved to a different molecule or within one molecule?
w: The reactant and product have the same formula; only the phosphate's position changes, so the enzyme rearranges a molecule into its isomer: an isomerase (a mutase). A transferase moves a group from one molecule to a different molecule.
x: A transferase moves a group to a different molecule. Here the phosphate moves to another carbon of the same molecule.
A ligase joins two molecules using ATP. Only one molecule is involved here, and its formula does not change.
A lyase adds or removes groups at a double bond, or breaks bonds without water. Compare the formulas of the reactant and product.

q: Which type of digestive enzyme hydrolyzes the phosphodiester bonds in DNA and RNA?
h: Enzyme names often tell the substrate: prote-, lip-, amyl- … Which matches nucleic acids?
w: A nuclease hydrolyzes the phosphodiester links in nucleic acids. Proteases break peptide bonds, lipases break the ester bonds of fats, and amylases break the glycosidic bonds of starch.
x: Proteases hydrolyze the peptide bonds in proteins. DNA and RNA are a different type of biomolecule.
Lipases hydrolyze the ester bonds in fats. Phosphodiester bonds are found in a different type of biomolecule.
Amylases hydrolyze the glycosidic bonds in starch. Think about which enzyme name matches nucleic acids.

q: An enzyme from a bacterium that lives in hot springs has its maximum activity at 75 °C. How does its activity at 37 °C compare?
c: Lower, because molecules collide less often and with less energy at 37 °C
Lower, because the enzyme is denatured at 37 °C
Higher, because 37 °C is the optimum for all enzymes
The same, because temperature does not affect enzymes below their optimum
h: On a rate-versus-temperature graph, what happens to the rate on the low-temperature side of the peak?
w: Below the optimum, the rate rises with temperature because more substrate collisions occur with enough energy. At 37 °C this enzyme is slower but not denatured; denaturation happens on the high-temperature side of the peak.
x: Denaturation happens when an enzyme is heated above its optimum. 37 °C is well below this enzyme's optimum of 75 °C.
37 °C is the optimum for most human enzymes, not all enzymes. This bacterial enzyme has its peak at 75 °C.
Below the optimum, temperature still matters: the rate rises as temperature rises toward the peak.

q: A noncompetitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction. On a graph of rate versus substrate concentration, how does the curve change?
c: The maximum rate is lower, even at very high substrate concentration.
The curve reaches the same maximum rate, but only at higher substrate concentration.
The maximum rate becomes higher than without the inhibitor.
The curve is unchanged because the inhibitor binds away from the active site.
h: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds outside the active site and changes the enzyme's shape. Can adding more substrate push it out?
w: The inhibitor changes the enzyme's shape, so some enzyme is inactive no matter how much substrate is added: the curve levels off at a lower maximum rate. Reaching the same maximum at higher substrate describes a competitive inhibitor.
x: Reaching the same maximum rate only at higher substrate is what a competitive inhibitor does, since substrate can push it out.
An inhibitor slows an enzyme; it never makes the maximum rate higher.
Binding away from the active site still changes the enzyme's shape, so the curve does change.

q: Sulfanilamide, an early antibiotic, has a structure very similar to PABA, a substrate bacteria use to make the vitamin folic acid. Sulfanilamide binds in the PABA site of the enzyme. What type of inhibitor is it?
h: Ask whether the inhibitor resembles the substrate and where on the enzyme it binds.
w: A molecule that looks like the substrate and competes for the active site is a competitive inhibitor; raising the PABA concentration can reduce its effect. Noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere on the enzyme.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds away from the active site. Sulfanilamide looks like PABA and binds in the PABA site.
An irreversible inhibitor forms a permanent covalent bond. Nothing here says sulfanilamide bonds covalently.
An activator speeds an enzyme up. Sulfanilamide slows the bacterial enzyme down.

q: Carbonic anhydrase is active only when a Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion is bound in its active site. Without the Zn<sup>2+</sup>, the inactive protein part is called the
h: A metal ion helper is a cofactor. What is the name for the protein alone, without its helper?
w: The protein portion alone is the apoenzyme; adding the cofactor (here the metal ion Zn2+) makes the active holoenzyme. A coenzyme is an organic helper, often made from a vitamin.
x: A coenzyme is an organic helper molecule, often made from a vitamin. The question asks for the name of the protein part alone.
The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on, not part of the enzyme.
Isoenzymes are different forms of an enzyme that catalyze the same reaction. That is not the protein without its metal ion.

q: The coenzyme FAD, which accepts hydrogen when a –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>– group is oxidized to –CH=CH–, is made from which vitamin?
h: Think of the name: FAD = flavin adenine dinucleotide.
w: The 'flavin' in FAD comes from riboflavin (vitamin B2). Niacin forms NAD+, and pantothenic acid forms coenzyme A.
x: Niacin (B<sub>3</sub>) is used to make NAD<sup>+</sup>, a different coenzyme. Think about the "flavin" in FAD.
Pantothenic acid (B<sub>5</sub>) is part of coenzyme A, not FAD.
Thiamine (B<sub>1</sub>) is used to make TPP, which helps remove CO<sub>2</sub>. It is not part of FAD.

q: Why must the B vitamins be eaten regularly, while vitamin A can be stored for months?
c: B vitamins are water-soluble and excreted in urine; vitamin A is fat-soluble and stored.
B vitamins are destroyed by stomach acid, while vitamin A passes through the stomach unchanged.
B vitamins are fat-soluble and burned for energy; vitamin A is water-soluble and recycled.
B vitamins act as enzymes that are used up in each reaction; vitamin A is never used up.
h: Group the vitamins by solubility. Which group dissolves in body fat, and which leaves the body easily?
w: B vitamins are water-soluble, so extra amounts are excreted in urine and must be replaced, while fat-soluble vitamin A is stored in fatty tissue and the liver. B vitamins act as coenzymes and are not consumed in each reaction.
x: The difference is not stomach acid. Sort the vitamins by solubility: which group can be stored in body fat?
This has the solubilities backward. Recall which vitamins dissolve in fat (A, D, E, K) and which in water.
B vitamins act as coenzymes, and coenzymes are not used up in each reaction. The real reason is how the body stores or excretes them.

q: Curve 1 shows the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction with no inhibitor. Curve 2 was measured with the same amount of enzyme after an inhibitor was added. What type of inhibitor is it?
h: Compare the two curves at very high substrate concentration. Can enough substrate overcome the inhibitor?
w: With the inhibitor (curve 2) the rate is lower at low [substrate], but at high [substrate] the two curves approach the same maximum rate. Extra substrate outcompetes the inhibitor for the active site, so it is a competitive inhibitor. A noncompetitive inhibitor would lower the maximum rate at every [substrate]; an irreversible inhibitor would not be reversed by substrate.
x: A noncompetitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate at every substrate concentration. Look at where the two curves end up at high [substrate].
Substrate cannot overcome an irreversible inhibitor, so the maximum rate would stay lower. Compare the curves at high [substrate].
An activator would make curve 2 faster than curve 1. Curve 2 is slower, at least at low [substrate].

q: Curve 1 is an enzyme working without inhibitor; curve 2 is the same enzyme with an inhibitor present. What does the graph show about the inhibitor?
c: It is noncompetitive; adding more substrate does not restore the maximum rate
It is competitive; adding more substrate restores the maximum rate
It is competitive; it lowers the maximum rate the enzyme can reach
It is noncompetitive; adding more substrate fully overcomes it
h: Look at the plateau of each curve. A plateau that stays lower no matter how much substrate is added means substrate cannot displace the inhibitor.
w: Curve 2 levels off at a lower maximum rate even when substrate is in large excess, so the inhibitor is not displaced by substrate: it binds somewhere other than the active site, a noncompetitive inhibitor. A competitive inhibitor would give a curve that eventually reaches the same plateau as curve 1.
x: If more substrate restored the maximum rate, the two curves would reach the same plateau. Check whether curve 2 catches up.
A competitive inhibitor does not lower the maximum rate; enough substrate can outcompete it. The type does not fit what the graph shows.
If more substrate fully overcame the inhibitor, curve 2 would eventually reach curve 1's plateau. Look at the two plateaus.

q: The graph shows reaction rate versus substrate concentration for a fixed amount of enzyme. Which change would significantly increase the rate at point c?
h: At point c the curve is flat. Ask what is limiting the rate there: the amount of substrate or the number of active sites?
w: At point c the enzyme is saturated: essentially every active site is occupied, so the curve has leveled off and the rate no longer depends on [substrate]. Only more enzyme (more active sites) raises the rate there. Adding substrate would only help at point a, where the curve is still rising steeply.
x: At point c the curve is flat, so more substrate barely changes the rate. Ask what is limiting the rate there.
A competitive inhibitor slows the enzyme; it cannot increase the rate.
At point c the enzyme is saturated, so removing some substrate would not raise the rate. It could only stay the same or drop.

q: The curves show the activity of three digestive enzymes as a function of pH. Which assignment is correct?
h: Match each optimum pH to the pH of the organ where the enzyme works: stomach acid is near pH 2; the small intestine is slightly basic.
w: Curve 1 peaks near pH 2, the pH of stomach acid, so it is pepsin; curve 3 peaks near pH 8, the slightly basic small intestine, so it is trypsin. Curve 2 (optimum near pH 7) fits salivary amylase. Reversing 1 and 3 is the common slip: trypsin is destroyed, not activated, by stomach acid.
x: This reverses the two. Curve 1 peaks near pH 2; ask which enzyme works in stomach acid.
Curve 2 peaks near pH 7, not pH 2, so it does not fit the stomach. Match each peak to the pH of each organ.
Curve 3 peaks near pH 8, which is too basic for the stomach. Match each peak to the pH of each organ.

q: The pH profile of an enzyme is shown. In which location would this enzyme most likely do its job?
h: Read the pH of maximum activity, then match it to the body compartment with that pH.
w: Activity peaks at about pH 8 and is nearly zero below pH 5, so the enzyme is built for a slightly basic environment: the small intestine, where pancreatic enzymes such as trypsin work. At blood pH (7.4) the enzyme would still be partly active, but its optimum is clearly higher.
x: This enzyme is almost inactive at pH 2. Read the pH where the curve peaks.
At pH 5 this enzyme has almost no activity. Read the pH where the curve peaks.
The enzyme is partly active at pH 7.4, but its peak is at a higher pH. Match the peak to a body location.

q: The graph shows the rate of a reaction catalyzed by a human enzyme at different temperatures. Why does the rate fall so sharply above about 40 °C?
c: The enzyme denatures, so its active site loses its shape
Molecules collide less often at higher temperature
The substrate is used up faster at higher temperature
Higher temperature turns the enzyme into a competitive inhibitor
h: Below the optimum, heat speeds collisions. Above it, heat does something to the protein itself.
w: Up to about 37–40 °C the rate rises because molecules move faster and collide more often. Above that, heat breaks the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold the protein's tertiary structure, so the enzyme denatures and the active site no longer fits the substrate. Collisions do not become rarer with heat; that answer reverses the kinetics.
x: Higher temperature makes molecules move faster and collide more often, not less. The drop comes from a change in the enzyme itself.
The steep drop happens even with plenty of substrate. Think about what heat does to a protein's shape.
Heat does not turn an enzyme into an inhibitor. Think about what heat does to the weak interactions that hold a protein's shape.

q: Curves 1 and 2 are temperature profiles of two enzymes that catalyze the same reaction: one from a human and one from a bacterium living in a hot spring. Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: Curve 1 is the human enzyme; it is denatured at the optimum temperature of enzyme 2
Curve 2 is the human enzyme; it is denatured at the optimum temperature of enzyme 1
Curve 1 is the human enzyme; the two enzymes share the same optimum temperature
Curve 2 is the human enzyme; it works fastest at about 75 °C
h: Human enzymes are tuned to body temperature, about 37 °C. Check what each curve does at the other curve's peak.
w: Curve 1 peaks near 37 °C (body temperature), so it is the human enzyme; curve 2 peaks near 75 °C, the hot-spring enzyme. At 75 °C curve 1 has dropped to zero: the human enzyme is denatured. The bacterial enzyme is simply slow, not denatured, at 37 °C.
x: Human enzymes work best near body temperature, 37 °C. Check which curve peaks near 37 °C.
The two curves peak at clearly different temperatures. Read the temperature at each peak.
Human enzymes work best near 37 °C, not 75 °C. Read which curve peaks near body temperature.

q: The energy diagram shows the same reaction with (curve 2) and without (curve 1) an enzyme. What does the enzyme change?
c: It lowers the activation energy; ΔH stays the same
It lowers ΔH; the activation energy stays the same
It makes ΔH more negative, releasing more energy
It raises the energy of the reactants to speed them up
h: Compare the two peaks, then compare where the two curves start and end.
w: Both curves start at the same reactant energy and end at the same product energy, so ΔH is unchanged (−20 kJ mol−1 either way). The enzyme provides a path with a lower peak: it lowers the activation energy. A catalyst never changes the energy of reactants or products, so it cannot make a reaction more exothermic.
x: Both curves start and end at the same energies, so ΔH is unchanged. Compare the heights of the two peaks instead.
A catalyst cannot change the energies of reactants or products, so the reaction does not become more exothermic.
Both curves start at the same reactant energy. The enzyme changes the pathway, not the energy of the reactants.

q: Use the energy diagram for a reaction run without enzyme (curve 1) and with enzyme (curve 2). By how much does the enzyme lower the activation energy?
h: Activation energy is measured from the reactants up to each peak. Subtract the two activation energies.
w: Ea(no enzyme) = 90 − 30 = 60 kJ mol−1; Ea(enzyme) = 55 − 30 = 25 kJ mol−1. The decrease is 60 − 25 = 35 kJ mol−1. 60 and 25 are the two activation energies themselves, not the difference; 45 comes from measuring the catalyzed peak from the products instead of the reactants.
x: 60 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> is the activation energy without the enzyme. The question asks how much the enzyme lowers it.
25 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> is the activation energy with the enzyme. Subtract it from the uncatalyzed activation energy.
This measures the catalyzed peak from the products instead of the reactants. Activation energy is measured from the reactants up to the peak.

q: Four descriptions of how an enzyme binds its substrate are listed in the table. Which one describes the induced-fit model?
h: Induced fit says the active site is flexible: binding the substrate changes the shape of the active site slightly.
w: In the induced-fit model the active site is not a rigid mold; it adjusts its shape as the substrate binds, so description II is correct. Description I is the older lock-and-key model (rigid, exact fit). III would change the primary structure, which binding never does; IV describes a non-specific enzyme, which contradicts enzyme specificity.

head: Description
rows: The active site is rigid and matches the substrate exactly, like a key in a lock
The active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, improving the fit
Binding the substrate changes the sequence of amino acids in the enzyme
Any molecule of about the right size can bind and be converted to product

x: A rigid active site that matches exactly, like a key in a lock, is the older lock-and-key model.
Substrate binding never changes the amino acid sequence (primary structure) of an enzyme.
Letting any molecule of about the right size bind goes against enzyme specificity. Neither model says this.

q: The table matches B vitamins to the coenzymes made from them. Which coenzyme belongs in the blank?
h: Which coenzyme carries acetyl and other acyl groups (as in acetyl CoA) and has pantothenic acid built into it?
w: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) is part of coenzyme A, the carrier of acyl groups such as the acetyl group in acetyl CoA. NADP+ and FMN are hydrogen carriers made from niacin and riboflavin, and pyridoxal phosphate (from vitamin B6) carries amino groups in transamination.
x: NADP<sup>+</sup> is a hydrogen carrier made from niacin. The blank needs a coenzyme that carries acyl groups.
FMN is a hydrogen carrier made from riboflavin. The blank needs a coenzyme that carries acyl groups.
Pyridoxal phosphate comes from vitamin B<sub>6</sub> and carries amino groups. Think about which coenzyme carries acetyl groups.

q: The table lists four enzymes and the helper each one needs to be active. Which two helpers are coenzymes made from vitamins?
h: Cofactors can be metal ions or small organic molecules. Only the organic ones (coenzymes) come from vitamins.
w: NAD+ (from niacin) and biotin (vitamin B7) are small organic molecules, so they are coenzymes derived from vitamins. Zn2+ and Mg2+ are inorganic metal-ion cofactors that come from minerals in the diet, not vitamins.
x: Zn<sup>2+</sup> and Mg<sup>2+</sup> are metal ions. Inorganic cofactors come from minerals, not vitamins.
NAD<sup>+</sup> is a vitamin-derived coenzyme, but Zn<sup>2+</sup> is an inorganic metal ion from minerals.
Biotin is a vitamin-derived coenzyme, but Mg<sup>2+</sup> is an inorganic metal ion from minerals.

q: In the pathway shown, the final product E binds to an allosteric site on enzyme 1 when E accumulates. Which statement describes this control?
c: Feedback inhibition: E slows enzyme 1, so less B, C and D are made
Competitive inhibition: E competes with A for the active site of enzyme 1
Feedback inhibition: E slows enzyme 4, the enzyme that makes E
Activation: E speeds up enzyme 1 so the cell makes more product
h: The end product regulates the FIRST enzyme, and it binds away from the active site (allosteric). What happens to everything downstream?
w: The end product binding an allosteric site on the first enzyme is feedback (end-product) inhibition: enzyme 1 slows, so B, C and D are all produced more slowly and the cell stops making E it does not need. Because E binds an allosteric site, not the active site, it is not competing with A. Inhibiting enzyme 4 would waste the intermediates already made.
x: E binds an allosteric site, not the active site, so it is not competing with A.
The end product regulates the first enzyme of the pathway. Slowing only the last step would waste the intermediates already made.
When the product accumulates, the cell needs less of it, not more. This control slows the pathway down.

q: A drug irreversibly inhibits enzyme 3 of the pathway shown. Which change in the concentrations of the intermediates is expected?
c: Z builds up and W is no longer made
W builds up and Z is no longer made
X builds up and Y, Z fall
Y builds up and Z, W rise
h: Find the step enzyme 3 catalyzes. Its substrate piles up; everything after it stops.
w: Enzyme 3 converts Z into W. Blocking it means Z accumulates (it is still made from Y but no longer used up) and W is no longer formed. Choosing W is the common mistake: the product of the blocked step disappears, it does not build up.
x: W is the product of the blocked step, so it disappears rather than building up. Z is still made, so think about what happens to it.
X and Y are made before enzyme 3, so the block does not stop their steps. Find the substrate of enzyme 3.
Blocking enzyme 3 stops W from forming, so W cannot rise. Find the step enzyme 3 catalyzes.

q: The cartoons show an enzyme interacting with a substrate (yellow) and an inhibitor (red). Which panel shows competitive inhibition?
h: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the same spot on the enzyme. Find the panel where the red molecule occupies that spot.
w: In panel III the red inhibitor sits in the active site and the yellow substrate is locked out, so inhibitor and substrate are competing for the same site: competitive inhibition. Panel IV is the tempting wrong pick: there the inhibitor is bound on the side of the enzyme and the active site is distorted (noncompetitive).
x: In panel IV the inhibitor is bound on the side of the enzyme, away from the active site, and warps the site. That is noncompetitive inhibition.
Panel II shows the substrate fitting in the active site with no inhibitor bound. Look for the red molecule.
Panel I shows the enzyme with no inhibitor bound. Look for the panel where the red molecule sits in the substrate's spot.

q: In each panel a red inhibitor molecule or a yellow substrate molecule approaches the same enzyme. Which panel shows noncompetitive inhibition?
h: A noncompetitive inhibitor never enters the active site. Look for an inhibitor bound elsewhere that has changed the shape of the site.
w: In panel II the red inhibitor is attached away from the active site, and the site has become warped so the substrate can no longer fit: noncompetitive inhibition. In panel I the inhibitor is inside the active site itself, which is competitive inhibition. Panels III and IV contain no inhibitor at all.
x: In panel I the inhibitor sits inside the active site, competing with the substrate. That is competitive inhibition.
Panel III shows a substrate fitting in the active site, with no inhibitor present.
Panel IV shows a substrate that does not fit the active site, with no inhibitor present.

q: Each panel is a snapshot of the same enzyme with a yellow molecule nearby. Which panel best illustrates the induced-fit model of enzyme action?
h: In induced fit the active site is flexible: binding the substrate makes the site change shape and close around it.
w: In panel IV the walls of the active site have tilted inward to hug the substrate: the site changed shape when the substrate bound, which is induced fit. Panel II is the common wrong choice: the substrate fits a rigid, unchanged site, which is the lock-and-key picture. Panel III shows a substrate that cannot bind at all.
x: In panel II the substrate fits a rigid, unchanged active site. That is the lock-and-key picture.
Panel I shows the enzyme with no substrate bound, so it cannot show the site changing shape around one.
Panel III shows a substrate that does not bind at all. Look for a site that has closed around its substrate.

q: The yellow shape is the substrate and the red shape is an inhibitor. Which panel shows an enzyme–substrate complex?
h: An enzyme–substrate complex forms when the substrate itself is bound in the active site, before any product is made.
w: Panel III shows the yellow substrate bound in the active site: the enzyme–substrate (ES) complex. Panel II looks similar but the red molecule in the site is an inhibitor, so it is an enzyme–inhibitor complex. Panel IV shows the products leaving after the reaction, and panel I is the free enzyme.
x: Panel II looks similar, but the molecule in the active site is the red inhibitor. That is an enzyme–inhibitor complex.
Panel I shows the free enzyme with nothing bound in the active site.
Panel IV shows products leaving after the reaction is over. Look for the substrate itself sitting in the active site.

q: Lettered labels mark parts of the drawings. Which label marks the active site of the enzyme?
c: a, the pocket in the top of the enzyme
b, the yellow molecule outside the enzyme
c, the red molecule sitting in the pocket
the entire blue body of the enzyme
h: The active site is a small region of the enzyme, not a separate molecule and not the whole protein.
w: The active site is the pocket (a) on the enzyme where the substrate binds. The yellow molecule (b) is the substrate and the red molecule (c) is an inhibitor, both separate molecules. A common misconception is that the whole enzyme is the active site; the site is only a small part of the large protein.
x: Label b is the yellow substrate, a separate molecule that binds to the enzyme. The active site is part of the enzyme itself.
Label c is the red inhibitor, a separate molecule. The active site is a region of the enzyme, not a molecule sitting in it.
The active site is only a small region of the large protein, not the whole enzyme.

q: In panel III, the red molecule is an inhibitor. It competes with…
c: the substrate, for the active site
the substrate, for a site away from the active site
the enzyme, for the substrate molecule
the product, for release from the enzyme
h: Look at where the red molecule is sitting and what the yellow molecule is waiting to do.
w: In panel III the inhibitor occupies the active site, the spot where the substrate (yellow) must bind, so inhibitor and substrate compete for the active site. Choosing "a site away from the active site" describes panel IV (noncompetitive). An inhibitor does not compete with the enzyme or with the product.
x: Binding at a site away from the active site describes noncompetitive inhibition (panel IV). Look at where the red molecule sits in panel III.
Inhibitors compete with something for a spot on the enzyme. They do not compete with the enzyme itself.
The product is released after the reaction; it is not what the inhibitor is competing with. Look at what the yellow molecule is waiting to do.

q: Two inhibited enzymes are drawn in panels II and III. Adding a large excess of substrate would restore the reaction rate in which panel, and why?
c: II, because substrate and inhibitor compete for the same site, so extra substrate wins the site more often
III, because the extra substrate crowds the inhibitor off its separate side site and frees the enzyme
II, because the extra substrate changes the shape of the inhibitor so it no longer fits the active site
III, because the extra substrate forces the distorted active site back into its original shape
h: Which inhibitor can be outcompeted? Substrate can only displace an inhibitor that is bound where the substrate itself binds.
w: In panel II the inhibitor is in the active site, competing with substrate; flooding the enzyme with substrate means the site is occupied by substrate most of the time, so the rate recovers (competitive inhibition is reversed by excess substrate). In panel III the inhibitor sits on a separate site and warps the active site; substrate cannot bind to the warped site at any concentration, so excess substrate does not help.
x: In panel III the inhibitor is on a separate site, so substrate cannot push it off. Substrate only displaces an inhibitor bound where substrate binds.
Substrate does not change the shape of the inhibitor. Think about why extra substrate helps when both molecules want the same site.
Substrate cannot bind a warped active site, so it cannot force the site back into shape. Adding substrate does not help in panel III.

q: Each enzyme catalyzes only one reaction or one type of reaction. Which panel illustrates the reason for this specificity?
h: Specificity means molecules of the wrong shape are rejected. Which panel shows a molecule that cannot enter the active site?
w: In panel I a triangular molecule is near the active site but its shape does not match the pocket, so it cannot bind and cannot react: the shape of the active site determines which substrate the enzyme accepts. Panels II and IV show the correct substrate binding and reacting, and panel III shows an empty enzyme. Picking II confuses binding of the right substrate with rejection of the wrong one.
x: Panel II shows the right substrate binding. Specificity is best shown by a molecule of the wrong shape being turned away.
Panel III shows an empty enzyme, so it does not show any molecule being accepted or rejected.
Panel IV shows products being released after the reaction. Look for a molecule that cannot fit the active site.

q: Panel I shows an enzyme at 37 °C with its substrate (yellow) bound. Panel II shows the same enzyme after it was heated to 80 °C for 10 minutes and then cooled. What happened to the enzyme in panel II?
c: Denaturation: heat broke the weak interactions holding the protein's folded shape
Noncompetitive inhibition: heat produced an inhibitor that bound to a side site
Saturation: the heat made the enzyme bind substrate too tightly to release it
Hydrolysis: heat broke the peptide bonds of the primary structure
h: Compare the shape of the protein in the two panels. Heat disrupts the weak interactions that hold the folded shape, not the covalent peptide backbone.
w: In panel II the protein chain has unfolded: there is no longer a pocket with the right shape, so the substrate cannot bind at all. Heat broke the hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and hydrophobic interactions that hold the tertiary structure, which is denaturation; for most enzymes it is not reversed by cooling. The peptide (covalent) bonds survive, so the primary structure is intact and this is not hydrolysis. No inhibitor molecule is present, so it is not inhibition.
x: No inhibitor molecule is present in panel II. Compare the overall shape of the protein in the two panels.
Saturation means all active sites are filled with substrate. In panel II the substrate cannot bind at all.
Heat at 80 °C breaks weak interactions, not the covalent peptide bonds. The primary structure stays intact, so this is not hydrolysis.

q: Of the four enzyme cartoons, which statement describes what is happening in panel IV?
c: The inhibitor occupies the active site, so the substrate cannot bind there
The inhibitor has bound outside the active site and changed the site's shape
The substrate is bound in the active site and is being converted to product
The enzyme has been permanently denatured by the inhibitor
h: Notice which molecule is inside the active site in panel IV and which one is waiting outside.
w: In panel IV the red inhibitor fills the active site and the yellow substrate is left outside, which is competitive inhibition. The statement about binding outside the site and reshaping it describes panel III (noncompetitive). Nothing in the drawing shows the enzyme unfolded, and a competitive inhibitor is usually reversible, so the enzyme is not permanently denatured.
x: Binding outside the active site and reshaping it describes panel III. Look at which molecule is inside the active site in panel IV.
In panel IV the substrate is outside the enzyme, not bound in the active site.
Nothing in panel IV shows the protein unfolded. The enzyme still has its shape; something is simply sitting in the active site.

q: A regulator molecule binds to an enzyme at a site that is not the active site. Binding changes the enzyme's shape so that the substrate no longer fits, slowing the reaction. Which panel shows this kind of regulation?
h: Find the panel where the regulating molecule is attached somewhere other than the active site, and the site itself has been distorted.
w: Panel III shows a molecule bound at a separate (allosteric) site, with the active site warped so the substrate cannot bind: this is allosteric regulation, the way many pathway end products shut off their own first enzyme. Panel I is the usual wrong choice, but there the molecule is inside the active site, which is competitive inhibition, not binding at a separate site.
x: In panel I the molecule sits inside the active site. The question describes binding at a site that is not the active site.
Panel II shows the substrate fitting in the active site, with no regulator bound.
Panel IV shows a substrate that does not fit, with no regulator bound. Look for a molecule attached away from the active site.

q: The panels show stages of enzyme action in scrambled order. Starting from the free enzyme, which order of panels shows one complete catalytic cycle?
h: An enzyme binds its substrate, converts it to product, releases the product, and is free to start again. An inhibitor is not part of this cycle.
w: The cycle is free enzyme (IV) → enzyme–substrate complex (I) → products released (III), after which the enzyme is free again. Panel II shows an inhibitor blocking the active site, which is not a step in catalysis, so any order including II is wrong. IV → III → I puts the products before the substrate has even bound.
x: Panel II shows an inhibitor blocking the active site, which is not a step in catalysis.
This order shows products released before the substrate has bound. Substrate binding must come first.
A cycle that starts from the free enzyme must begin with the panel where nothing is bound. Find that panel first.

q: A lab measures the rate of an enzyme reaction while the amount of enzyme is increased and the substrate is kept in large excess. Which curve shows the expected result?
h: With substrate in excess every enzyme molecule is kept busy. Twice the enzyme means twice as many active sites working.
w: With excess substrate each added enzyme molecule immediately finds substrate, so the rate is directly proportional to the enzyme amount: a straight line through the origin, curve I. Curve II is the tempting mix-up: it is the shape of rate versus substrate concentration, where the enzyme (not the substrate) becomes the limit. Curve IV is the shape of a temperature or pH profile.
x: Curve II levels off, which is the shape of rate versus substrate concentration. Here substrate is in excess, so nothing runs out.
Curve III is flat, meaning adding enzyme would not change the rate at all. With excess substrate, more enzyme means more active sites working.
Curve IV is bell-shaped, the shape of a temperature or pH profile. Adding enzyme does not have an optimum amount.

q: The graph shows the rate of an enzyme reaction versus substrate concentration for a fixed amount of enzyme; the dashed line is the maximum rate. Why does the rate rise much less between 16 and 20 mM substrate than between 0 and 4 mM?
c: At high substrate most active sites are already filled, so extra substrate adds little
At high substrate the extra substrate begins to denature the enzyme molecules
At high substrate the substrate starts to act as a competitive inhibitor
At high substrate the enzyme is used up as it is converted into product
h: With a fixed amount of enzyme there is a fixed number of active sites. What happens when nearly all of them are busy?
w: From 0 to 4 mM the rate jumps from 0 to about 40 μmol min−1, but from 16 to 20 mM it only creeps from about 64 to 67 as it approaches the dashed maximum. At high substrate most active sites are already occupied, so the enzyme is nearly saturated and extra substrate adds little. Only more enzyme would raise the maximum. Enzymes are not used up or denatured by their substrate.
x: Substrate does not denature enzymes; heat and extreme pH do. Think about how many active sites are free at high substrate.
The substrate is what the enzyme acts on, not an inhibitor. Think about the fixed number of active sites.
Enzymes are catalysts and are not used up. The limit comes from how many active sites are already busy.

q: Curve 1 is an enzyme with no inhibitor. Curve 2 was run with an inhibitor, and curve 3 with twice as much of the same inhibitor. Which conclusion do the curves support?
c: Competitive: more inhibitor means more substrate is needed to reach a given rate, but the same maximum is still approached
Noncompetitive: more inhibitor lowers the maximum rate the enzyme can reach, in proportion to the amount added
Irreversible: at the higher level used for curve 3 the enzyme molecules have been permanently destroyed
Competitive: the inhibitor lowers the maximum rate the enzyme can reach, and more inhibitor lowers it further
h: Compare where the three curves are heading at high substrate concentration, and how far each is shifted to the right at low concentration.
w: All three curves climb toward the same dashed maximum rate at high substrate concentration; the inhibitor only shifts the curve to the right, and doubling the inhibitor (curve 3) shifts it further than curve 2. Because a large excess of substrate overcomes the inhibitor, it is competitive. A noncompetitive inhibitor would give lower plateaus, and an irreversible inhibitor would not be overcome by added substrate.
x: If the inhibitor were noncompetitive, curves 2 and 3 would level off at lower plateaus. Look at where all three curves are heading.
An irreversible inhibitor could not be overcome by adding substrate. Check whether curve 3 still approaches the same maximum.
A competitive inhibitor does not lower the maximum rate. Look at the plateaus of the three curves at high substrate.

q: Lysosomes are acidic compartments inside cells (pH about 5) that break down worn-out cell parts. The graph shows pH profiles of four enzymes. Which curve most likely belongs to a lysosomal enzyme?
h: Each enzyme works fastest at the pH of the place where it normally acts. Find the curve whose peak sits at about pH 5.
w: A lysosomal enzyme is most active at the lysosome's pH, so its peak should be near pH 5: curve 2. Curve 1 (peak near pH 2) fits a stomach enzyme such as pepsin; curve 3 (near 7.4) fits an enzyme of blood or cytoplasm; curve 4 (near 9.5) fits an enzyme that works in strongly basic conditions. Students who assume "acidic" means the most acidic curve pick 1, but pH 2 is far more acidic than a lysosome.
x: Curve 1 peaks near pH 2, which fits the stomach. A lysosome, at pH about 5, is much less acidic than that.
Curve 3 peaks near pH 7.4, which fits blood or cytoplasm. Find the curve that peaks near pH 5.
Curve 4 peaks near pH 9.5, which is basic. A lysosome is acidic, at about pH 5.

q: Curve 1 is a human enzyme and curve 2 is the matching enzyme from a cold-water fish. At which temperature are both enzymes working at more than half of their maximum rate?
h: Follow the 50 % line across the graph and note where each curve lies above it. Only one of the listed temperatures is inside both ranges.
w: At 25 °C curve 1 (human) is at about 75 % and curve 2 (fish) at about 70 %, so both are above half-maximum. At 15 °C the fish enzyme is near its peak but the human enzyme is below 40 %; at 35 °C the human enzyme is near its maximum but the fish enzyme has already denatured and is close to zero; at 45 °C the human enzyme is collapsing and the fish enzyme is completely inactive.
x: At 15 °C the fish enzyme is near its peak, but the human enzyme is below half its maximum.
At 35 °C the human enzyme is near its maximum, but the fish enzyme has already denatured and is close to zero.
At 45 °C the human enzyme is already falling, and the fish enzyme is completely inactive.

q: A sample of a human enzyme is held at 60 °C for 15 minutes, cooled back to 37 °C, and then its rate is measured. Using the temperature profile shown, what rate is expected, and why?
c: Far below the value shown at 37 °C, because heat unfolded the protein and cooling does not refold it
The value shown at 37 °C, because the drop at 60 °C was only molecules moving too fast to bind and cooling reverses it
Above the value shown at 37 °C, because the enzyme stored extra heat energy that speeds up catalysis
The value shown at 60 °C, because an enzyme's rate is fixed by the highest temperature it has ever reached
h: The sharp collapse above the optimum is denaturation, a change in the protein's shape. Ask whether that change undoes itself on cooling.
w: The steep fall above about 45 °C is denaturation: the heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the active site's shape, and for most enzymes this unfolding is not reversed by cooling, so the sample stays nearly inactive at 37 °C. The tempting wrong answer treats the drop like the slow rates at low temperature, which are reversible because the enzyme is still folded. Enzymes do not store heat energy.
x: The steep drop above the optimum is not from molecules moving too fast; it is a change in the protein's shape. Ask whether cooling undoes that.
Enzymes do not store heat energy. Think about what high heat does to the protein's folded shape.
A rate is not fixed by the highest temperature reached. What matters is whether the protein still has its folded shape.

q: The graph shows the amount of product formed over time in an enzyme-catalyzed reaction that started with 40 μmol of substrate. What is the initial rate of the reaction?
h: Rate = slope of the product-versus-time line. Use the straight early part of the curve, before the substrate runs low.
w: During the first few minutes the line is straight: about 20 μmol of product form in the first 4 min, so the initial rate is 20 μmol / 4 min = 5 μmol min−1. The curve is straight at first because the enzyme is saturated with substrate; it flattens later because the substrate is used up. Dividing the final 40 μmol by 20 min (2 μmol min−1) averages over the time when the reaction had already slowed; 20 μmol min−1 reads the product at 4 min as if it were a rate.
x: This divides the final 40 μmol by 20 min, averaging in the time when the reaction had already slowed. Use the straight early part of the curve.
This reads the product made at 4 min as if it were a rate. Divide the product formed by the time it took.
40 μmol is the total substrate, not a rate. Find the slope of the straight early part of the curve.

q: Reaction 1 and reaction 2 convert the same substrate to the same product. What does the shape of curve 2 indicate about reaction 2?
c: It is not catalyzed by an enzyme; with no active sites to fill, the rate just rises with the number of substrate collisions
It is catalyzed by an enzyme with a larger maximum rate than the enzyme in reaction 1
It is catalyzed by an enzyme that reaches half of its maximum rate at a lower substrate concentration than the enzyme in reaction 1
It is catalyzed by the same enzyme as reaction 1 but with a competitive inhibitor present
h: Every enzyme has a limited number of active sites, so an enzyme-catalyzed rate must eventually level off. What kind of reaction never saturates?
w: An enzyme has a fixed number of active sites, so at high substrate concentration they are all occupied and the rate levels off (curve 1). Curve 2 is a straight line that never levels off, so there is no saturable catalyst: reaction 2 is an uncatalyzed reaction whose rate simply grows with the collision frequency. A faster enzyme or one that is half-saturated at lower substrate would still give a curve that bends toward a plateau, and a competitive inhibitor would make curve 2 lie below curve 1 at low substrate but still level off.
x: Any enzyme, however fast, would still give a curve that bends toward a plateau once its active sites fill. Curve 2 never levels off.
An enzyme that is half-saturated at lower substrate would still bend toward a plateau. Curve 2 is a straight line.
With a competitive inhibitor, the enzyme would still level off at high substrate. Curve 2 never bends.

q: A purified enzyme was treated to remove any bound metal ions, then its activity was measured alone and after adding different ions. What do the results show?
c: Mg<sup>2+</sup> is a required cofactor of the enzyme, and the other ions cannot take its place
Zn<sup>2+</sup> and Ca<sup>2+</sup> are inhibitors that shut the enzyme down
Mg<sup>2+</sup> is a coenzyme that the enzyme uses as a source of energy
Mg<sup>2+</sup> is the substrate of the enzyme, so adding it raises the rate
h: Compare the metal-free bar with each added-ion bar. Only one ion changes the activity. Is a metal ion a cofactor or a coenzyme?
w: Without any ion the enzyme is almost inactive; adding Mg2+ restores full activity while Zn2+ and Ca2+ leave it as low as the metal-free control, so Mg2+ is a required cofactor and the other ions cannot substitute for it. They are not inhibitors because they did not lower activity below the control. A metal ion is a cofactor, not a coenzyme; coenzymes are organic molecules made from vitamins.
x: Zn<sup>2+</sup> and Ca<sup>2+</sup> did not lower activity below the metal-free control, so they are not acting as inhibitors.
A metal ion is a cofactor, not a coenzyme; coenzymes are organic molecules made from vitamins. Mg<sup>2+</sup> is also not an energy source.
The enzyme was nearly inactive without any metal ion. That points to a helper the enzyme needs, not a substrate that gets converted.

q: The graph follows the activity of an enzyme solution over time. Hg<sup>2+</sup> ions were added at 2 min, and at 6 min the solution was dialyzed, which removed all free Hg<sup>2+</sup>. What type of inhibition does the graph show?
c: Irreversible (noncompetitive) inhibition: Hg<sup>2+</sup> bonds to –SH groups of cysteine side chains and permanently changes the enzyme's shape
Competitive inhibition: Hg<sup>2+</sup> resembles the substrate and occupies the active site until it is removed
Reversible inhibition: Hg<sup>2+</sup> binds loosely to a side site and leaves when its concentration drops
Feedback inhibition: Hg<sup>2+</sup> is the end product of the pathway and signals the enzyme to stop
h: A reversible inhibitor leaves the enzyme once it is removed from the solution. Check whether the activity came back after dialysis.
w: Activity drops when Hg2+ is added and stays near zero after dialysis removes the free Hg2+, so the inhibitor remains bonded to the enzyme: it is held by strong covalent bonds, typically to the –SH groups of cysteine, which is irreversible inhibition. Hg2+ does not compete with the substrate for the active site, so heavy metals are also classed as noncompetitive inhibitors. A reversibly bound inhibitor would release the enzyme, so the activity would climb back after dialysis. Heavy-metal ions are not pathway products, so this is not feedback inhibition.
x: Hg<sup>2+</sup> does not look like the substrate, and a competitive inhibitor comes off when it is removed, so activity would have recovered after dialysis.
If Hg<sup>2+</sup> were only loosely bound, dialysis would have pulled it off and activity would have climbed back. It stayed near zero.
Feedback inhibition is a pathway's own end product switching off an early enzyme. Hg<sup>2+</sup> is a toxic metal ion, not a product of the pathway.

q: A nursing student says that enzymes are "used up" by the reactions they speed up. Which statement about enzymes is actually correct?
c: They are proteins that speed up a reaction without being used up
They are carbohydrates that supply energy to a reaction
They shift the equilibrium so that more product forms
They are consumed in the reaction, so more must be eaten daily
h: Enzymes are biological catalysts. What is a catalyst made of in the body, and what does a catalyst do and not do?
w: Enzymes are globular proteins that act as catalysts: they lower the activation energy and are released unchanged, so one enzyme molecule can be reused thousands of times. A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or the energy difference between reactants and products, only how fast equilibrium is reached. Vitamins, not enzymes, must be eaten.
x: Enzymes are proteins, not carbohydrates, and they do not supply energy to the reaction.
A catalyst speeds forward and reverse reactions equally, so it does not shift the equilibrium.
This repeats the student's misconception. Catalysts come out of the reaction unchanged and can be reused.

q: Four digestive enzymes are matched in the table with the bond each one hydrolyzes and the nutrient it digests. Which enzyme replaces the question mark?
h: Match the name to the substrate: -ase added to the thing it works on, or a name based on protein, fat, starch or nucleic acid.
w: Peptide (amide) bonds between amino acids are hydrolyzed by proteases such as pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin. Lipases hydrolyze the ester bonds of fats, amylase hydrolyzes the α(1→4) bonds of starch, and nucleases hydrolyze the phosphodiester bonds of DNA and RNA.
x: Lipases hydrolyze ester bonds in fats; that row already has an enzyme. The blank row hydrolyzes peptide bonds.
Amylase hydrolyzes glycosidic bonds in starch. The blank row hydrolyzes peptide (amide) bonds.
Nucleases hydrolyze phosphodiester bonds in DNA and RNA. The blank row hydrolyzes the bonds in proteins.

q: Lactate dehydrogenase, an enzyme measured in blood tests for tissue damage, catalyzes the reaction drawn. To which class of enzymes does it belong?
h: Look at what happens to the –OH carbon: it becomes C=O while NAD<sup>+</sup> picks up the hydrogen.
w: A secondary alcohol (–CH(OH)–) is converted to a ketone (C=O) and the hydrogens are transferred to NAD+, so the reaction is an oxidation–reduction and the enzyme is an oxidoreductase (dehydrogenases belong here). Nothing is rearranged within one molecule (isomerase), no water is used to split a bond (hydrolase) and no group is removed to form a double bond (lyase).
x: An isomerase rearranges atoms within one molecule without changing its formula. Here H is removed and given to NAD<sup>+</sup>.
A hydrolase uses water to split a bond. No water is used and the molecule is not split.
A lyase removes a group to form a C=C or adds one to it. Here a C–OH becomes C=O, with hydrogen going to NAD<sup>+</sup>.

q: A liver esterase breaks down the ester shown (a food flavoring) in the reaction drawn. In which of the six enzyme classes is this esterase placed?
h: The reagent over the arrow is water, and the ester splits into two pieces. Which enzyme class uses water to break bonds?
w: The ester bond is split by water into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, which is hydrolysis, so the enzyme is a hydrolase (lipases, proteases and amylases are also hydrolases). A ligase joins two molecules using ATP, a transferase moves a group from one molecule to another and an oxidoreductase changes oxidation state.
x: A ligase joins two molecules using ATP. Here one molecule is split into two by water.
A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Look at the reagent over the arrow: water splits the ester.
An oxidoreductase changes oxidation state, usually with NAD<sup>+</sup> or FAD. No redox coenzyme is involved here.

q: Rickets is a childhood disease in which bones stay soft and bend because too little calcium is deposited in them. A deficiency of which vitamin causes rickets, and what is that vitamin’s role?
c: Vitamin D; it is needed to absorb calcium and phosphate for bone
Vitamin A; it is needed to make the visual pigment in the retina
Vitamin K; it is needed to make blood-clotting proteins
Vitamin B<sub>1</sub>; it is converted to a coenzyme for decarboxylation
h: Which fat-soluble vitamin is made in skin exposed to sunlight and controls blood calcium?
w: Rickets (soft, bending bones) is caused by a lack of vitamin D, which the body needs to absorb Ca2+ and phosphate from the intestine and deposit them in bone. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, and B vitamins are water-soluble coenzyme precursors.
x: Vitamin A is needed for vision; a deficiency causes night blindness, not soft bones.
Vitamin K is needed for clotting; a deficiency causes bleeding, not soft bones.
Thiamine (B<sub>1</sub>) is a water-soluble coenzyme precursor. Rickets involves calcium and bone, which points to a fat-soluble vitamin.

q: A nutrition handout pairs four vitamins with a claimed function (table). Which pairing is correct?
h: A, D, E and K are fat-soluble with specific jobs (vision, bone, clotting); the B vitamins become coenzymes.
w: Row II is correct: vitamin K is required to make the clotting factors, so a deficiency causes bleeding. Row I has the roles of A and D reversed (A is for vision, D for calcium and bone); row III is wrong because niacin (B3) is the precursor of NAD+, not of FAD (that is riboflavin, B2); row IV is wrong because vitamin D is fat-soluble and is stored.

head: Row
Vitamin
Function stated
rows: absorption of calcium for strong bones
water-soluble; excess is lost in urine daily

x: Row I gives vitamin A the job of vitamin D. Vitamin A is needed for vision.
Niacin (B<sub>3</sub>) is the precursor of NAD<sup>+</sup>. FAD comes from riboflavin (B<sub>2</sub>).
Vitamin D is fat-soluble and can be stored in the body, so excess is not lost in urine each day.

q: A patient takes a drug that is a competitive inhibitor of an enzyme. After a meal, the concentration of the enzyme's natural substrate rises sharply. What happens to the degree of inhibition, and why?
c: It decreases, because substrate outcompetes the drug for the active site
It increases, because more substrate means more enzyme–inhibitor complexes
It is unchanged, because the drug binds at an allosteric site
It becomes permanent, because the substrate traps the drug in the active site
h: Competitive inhibitors and substrate fight for the same spot. Which wins when the substrate concentration is much higher?
w: Substrate and a competitive inhibitor bind the same active site, so raising [substrate] shifts the competition toward enzyme–substrate complexes and the inhibition decreases (the maximum rate can still be reached). Inhibition unaffected by substrate describes a noncompetitive inhibitor, which binds away from the active site; permanent loss describes an irreversible inhibitor.
x: More substrate means more enzyme–substrate complexes, not more enzyme–inhibitor complexes. Both are competing for the same site.
A competitive inhibitor binds the active site, not an allosteric site. Binding there means substrate concentration matters.
Substrate does not trap a competitive inhibitor; competitive binding is reversible. Permanent loss would describe an irreversible inhibitor.

q: The pancreas makes the protein-digesting enzyme trypsin as an inactive zymogen, trypsinogen, which is switched on only in the small intestine. Why is this important?
c: It keeps trypsin from digesting the proteins of the pancreas itself
Trypsinogen digests proteins faster than trypsin
It allows trypsin to work in the acid of the stomach
Zymogens can pass through cell membranes, but enzymes cannot
h: Trypsin hydrolyzes peptide bonds. What else is made of proteins besides food?
w: An active protease made in the pancreas would hydrolyze the pancreas's own proteins. Making it as an inactive zymogen and activating it only in the small intestine protects the pancreas. Activation cuts off a piece of the chain (hydrolysis of a peptide bond).
x: A zymogen is inactive. It must be activated before it can digest anything.
Trypsin works in the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, not in the acid of the stomach.
Zymogens are secreted from cells like other proteins. The point is that they are inactive until they reach the right place.

q: Glycogen phosphorylase is switched on when a kinase attaches a phosphate group to a serine side chain of the enzyme, and switched off when a phosphatase removes the phosphate. This type of regulation is called
c: allosteric control by a regulator that binds without forming a covalent bond
feedback inhibition by the end product of the pathway
h: Is a covalent bond formed to the enzyme, and can the change be undone?
w: Adding or removing a phosphate group through a covalent bond is covalent modification. Phosphorylation is reversible: a kinase adds the phosphate, and a phosphatase takes it off.
x: An allosteric regulator binds reversibly through weak attractions at a regulatory site. Here a phosphate group is covalently bonded to the enzyme.
