In feedback inhibition, the end product of a pathway binds to an earlier enzyme. Here a phosphate is attached by another enzyme.
Zymogen activation cuts a peptide bond and cannot be undone. Phosphorylation can be reversed by a phosphatase.

q: Which statement correctly compares zymogen activation with phosphorylation as ways of turning enzymes on?
c: Zymogen activation cuts a peptide bond and cannot be reversed; phosphorylation can be reversed by a phosphatase
Both can be reversed easily within seconds
Zymogen activation adds a phosphate group; phosphorylation cuts a peptide bond
Neither involves forming or breaking a covalent bond
h: What happens to the protein chain in each case, and can it be put back?
w: Activating a zymogen hydrolyzes a peptide bond and removes a piece of the chain, so it is one-way. Phosphorylation adds a phosphate that a phosphatase can remove, so it is reversible. Zymogen activation is permanent; phosphorylation is reversible.
x: Once the blocking piece of a zymogen is cut off, it cannot be reattached, so zymogen activation is not reversible.
This swaps the two. Phosphorylation adds a phosphate group; zymogen activation cuts a peptide bond.
Both are covalent changes: one breaks a peptide bond and the other forms a phosphate ester bond.

q: Some California workers who mix and apply organophosphate pesticides have the cholinesterase activity of their blood checked. After a spraying season, a worker's result is well below the worker's own starting value. What does this most likely mean?
c: The pesticide has bonded covalently to the enzyme's active site and inhibited it
His body has made extra cholinesterase to protect itself
His blood is low in acetylcholine
The pesticide has been hydrolyzed by the enzyme and is now harmless
h: Organophosphates bond to a serine –OH in the active site of cholinesterase. What does that do to enzyme activity?
w: Organophosphates form a covalent bond to the active-site serine of cholinesterase, which is irreversible inhibition, so measured activity drops. A fall from the worker's own starting value is a warning of exposure, even before symptoms appear.
x: Making more enzyme would raise the activity, not lower it.
The test measures the enzyme's activity. When the enzyme is blocked, acetylcholine tends to build up rather than fall.
The organophosphate stays bonded to the enzyme and blocks it. A lower activity means the enzyme is inhibited.

q: Acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that organophosphate pesticides block, normally adds water to break the ester bond of acetylcholine, giving choline and acetic acid. To which enzyme class does it belong?
h: Which class of enzyme uses water to split a bond?
w: Breaking a bond by adding water is hydrolysis, so acetylcholinesterase is a hydrolase. When it is blocked, acetylcholine is not broken down, and nerves keep firing.
x: Oxidoreductases move electrons or hydrogen, as dehydrogenases do. Hydrolysis of an ester is not a redox reaction.
A transferase moves a group from one molecule to another. Here water splits one molecule into two.
A ligase joins two molecules using ATP. Acetylcholinesterase splits a molecule.

q: Fluconazole treats Valley fever by binding to a fungal enzyme in the pathway that makes ergosterol. Why does it harm the fungus much more than the patient?
c: It binds the fungal enzyme much more tightly than the matching human enzyme, because the enzymes' shapes differ
It denatures every protein it touches
Humans need ergosterol in their diet
h: Enzymes are specific: a drug fits the active site of one enzyme better than another.
w: Enzyme action depends on the shape of the active site. The fungal enzyme and its human counterpart differ in shape, so fluconazole binds the fungal enzyme far more tightly. That specificity is what makes it a useful drug.
x: Human cells have membranes too; they use cholesterol instead of ergosterol.
A drug that denatured all proteins would harm the patient as much as the fungus.
Humans do not use ergosterol in their membranes. The selectivity comes from the drug binding the fungal enzyme.
